title: Australian Rock

paragraphs.text: The Gwion rock art found across Western Australia's remote Kimberley region is not only beautiful and mysterious, it also holds vital clues to humanity's distant past. Teams of archaeologists and scientists have been attracted to the area in an attempt to understand more about these ancient wonders. The mysterious Gwion rock paintings are thought to be at least 17,000 years old, perhaps more than 25,000 years old. No one knows who painted these little-known Gwions-some small, others up to five metres long and three metres high-which lie deliberately hidden in inaccessible rock shelters in the vast Kimberley, an area three times the size of England. Researchers believe there are probably hundreds of thousands of Gwion paintings but concede that they will never find them all.

What is known, however, is that Before the last Ice Age, people with developed artistic skills came to the Kimberley and painted this highly distinctive rock art. The figures portray an early civilisation in Australia living through climate change-from leisurely days of abundance to fear and fighting at the start of the last Ice Age The earliest eras of Gwion painting depict highly decorated people and their ceremonies. However, in the last scenes we have of the Gwion world. The people are without adornments on the body and are portrayed running and hunting. Aggressive groups are shown in battle, presumably fighting over rapidly diminishing supplies and the last remains of favourable territory. At that time, conditions became so harsh and arid that the majority of the population left the Kimberley, which remained largely abandoned for the next 8,000 to 10,000 years. The Gwion artists disappeared, leaving their magnificent paintings, but barely any other trace of their existence. Gwion rock art ceased as suddenly as it had begun.

At first glimpse, the Gwion Paintings appeared very different from the Wandjina rock art found in the same area. The Wandjina figures are abstract faces depicted with large eyes and no mouths. They date from 3,500 years ago, and are still part of Aboriginal culture today. Because of this difference, a controversial theory arose that suggested the Gwion art was painted by a mystery race. While scientists are unable to agree on this theory, they are keen to continue studying these ancient artists to try to understand what became of them. They hope that these paintings could help resolve some of the critical debates in the world of archaeology regarding the timing, route and pace of modern human movement out of Africa, and then via Asia and Indonesia to Australia. They also believe their studies of Gwion art may hold the answers to how earlier people responded to major changes in climate, and how they moved to and from neighbouring countries.

This search for answers has attracted a stream of enthusiastic followers. Gwion art written history only begins in 1891, when Joseph Bradshaw became the first European to document this stylish rock art. Other notable researchers in this area include German Dr Helmut Petri, but it was the amateur Australian archaeologist, Graeme Walsh, whose name became synonymous with Gwion art. In 1977, Walsh began a 30-year campaign to search the Kimberley for rock art. He meticulous photographed, produced sketches and documented his extensive amateur field research, identifying some 300 recurring motifs in the paintings, the meanings of which he sought to interpret. Walsh became absorbed with the notion that Gwion art was markedly different from the Wandjina rock art that followed later.

Walsh then proposed his controversial hypothesis: instead of Australia being continuously settled for 50,000 to 55,000 years by ancestors of contemporary Aboriginal Australians, Walsh suggested that there were a number of distinct stages in the migration of people to Australia, and one of these could have been people of a different ethnic identity, who create the Gwions. Academic anthropologists and archaeologists, while acknowledging the immense value of Walsh's field work, largely discredited his pre-aboriginal civilisation' theory. Many cited similarities with the dynamic Aboriginal Mimi rock art in Arnhem Land in the north of Australia, and with Aboriginal ceremonial dress still used in some regions today.

A major obstacle in understanding The Gwions is the lack of accurate Dates. For radiocarbon dating of paintings to be successful, the paint should contain organic material, such as animal fat, plant material or blood, unfortunately no such sample has been found. Presently, there is only one published scientific date to establish Gwions age-17, 400 years old- recorded in 1995 after a fossilized wasps nest covering a Gwion figure was dated. However, this only determined a minimum age of 17, 400 years from the time the wasp built its nest, so the paintings could be much older.

Despite practical difficulties and differences of opinion, researchers are eager to tell the story of Gwion art. Their investigations into these paintings will hopefully answer a wide range of fundamental questions relating to the cultural history of human settlement in Australia's Kimberley region, and the climatic and ecological contexts in which it developed.
